motivation: Automotive software updates are slow and require extensive re-validation; hotpatching could speed up updates but existing solutions lack safety compliance and support for flash-based XIP architectures.
method: The authors designed Patchlings, a hotpatching framework that operates on flash-based Execute-in-Place (XIP) systems, and implemented it on NXP S32K148EVB with FreeRTOS and Zephyr.
result: Patchlings achieves low deterministic overhead (e.g., 3.3 µs patch application), small firmware size increase (as low as 6.34%), and successfully patches real CVEs.
conclusion: Patchlings demonstrates the feasibility of safe, persistent hotpatching for automotive ECUs, potentially reducing mean-time-to-mitigate for vulnerabilities.

title: Symmetry Defeats Auditing
authors: Zeke Medley Nick Merrill
abstract: ArXiv:2605.27836v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We demonstrate an attack on Introspection Adapters (Shenoy et al., 2026).
tldr: This paper presents an attack on Introspection Adapters, a topic unrelated to the user's research interests.
motivation: The research was conducted to demonstrate a security vulnerability in a specific AI auditing technique.

title: Can It Reach The Generator? Investigating The Survival Of Prompt-Injection Attacks In Realistic Rag Settings
authors: Yu Yin, Shuai Wang, Bevan Koopman, Guido Zuccon
abstract: ArXiv:2605.28017v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent generative engine optimisation (GEO) research has shown that prompt-injection attacks can push a target product to the top of an LLM's recommendation list, with the strongest attacks reporting around [MATH] success and raising serious security concerns about RAG-based recommendation. However, these results assume the attacked document is always fed directly to the generator, bypassing the retriever and reranker. This is unrealistic: in deployed RAG systems, the attack modifies the document content, which can in turn change whether the document is retrieved and reranked highly enough to reach the generator at all. In this paper, we re-evaluate seven GEO attacks under a realistic three-stage pipeline (retriever\,[MATH]\,LLM reranker\,[MATH]\,LLM generator). We find that prior protocols substantially overstate attack effectiveness: gradient-based and instruction override attacks largely collapse before reaching the generator, and only LLM-driven prompt injections remain effective end-to-end. Our analysis further reveals that current GEO attacks are easily detectable: a lightweight prompt-injection guard finetuned on a small attack dataset already detects every attack. Our code and data are available at [URL].
tldr: This paper evaluates the effectiveness of prompt-injection attacks in realistic RAG systems, finding that most attacks fail after retrieval and reranking, and are easily detectable.
motivation: Prior work on generative engine optimization (GEO) assumed attacked documents bypass retrieval and reranking, overstating attack success. This study aims to assess attacks under realistic RAG pipelines.
method: The authors re-evaluate seven GEO attacks in a three-stage pipeline (retriever, LLM reranker, LLM generator) and test detection using a lightweight prompt-injection guard.
result: Gradient-based and instruction override attacks collapse before reaching the generator; only LLM-driven prompt injections remain effective. All attacks are detectable by a small finetuned guard.
conclusion: Current GEO attacks are less threatening than previously thought, and simple defenses can detect them. Future work should focus on more robust attacks and defenses.

title: AgentGuard: An Attribute-Based Access Control Framework For Tool-Use LLM-Based Agent
authors: Jiaqi Luo, Songyang Peng, Jiarun Dai, Zhile Chen, Zhuoxiang Shen, Geng Hong, Xudong Pan, Yuan Zhang, Min Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2605.28071v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-based agents have recently attracted significant attention due to their ability to autonomously invoke relevant tools to accomplish complex tasks. However, recent studies have shown that these agents face severe security risks, which may lead to privacy leakage, financial loss, or even full system compromise. In this paper, we present AgentGuard, an attribute-based access control framework for tool-use LLM-based agents. AgentGuard adopts a client-server architecture. On the client side, AgentGuard provides lightweight integration for agents implemented in different programming languages and architectures. It requires only minor code modifications (e.g., around 10 lines) without changing the underlying agent execution logic. On the server side, AgentGuard provides three complementary inspection mechanisms to cover both single-tool and cross-tool security risks in agent execution. In addition, it offers a visualized front-end interface for security policy specification and runtime auditing. Currently, AgentGuard is publicly accessible at [URL].
tldr: AgentGuard is an attribute-based access control framework for securing LLM-based agents that use external tools.
motivation: LLM-based agents face severe security risks such as privacy leakage and financial loss when invoking tools; existing solutions lack fine-grained access control.
method: The framework uses a client-server architecture with lightweight client integration and server-side inspection mechanisms for single-tool and cross-tool risks, plus a visual policy specification interface.
result: AgentGuard provides effective security enforcement with minimal code changes (around 10 lines) and no modification to agent execution logic.
conclusion: The framework offers a practical solution for securing tool-use LLM agents, with potential for broader adoption in agent-based systems.

title: Mirage: Context-Aware Prompt Injection Against Mobile Gui Agents Via User-Generated Content
authors: Ruoqi Guo, Yi Liu, Gelei Deng, Yiheng Xiong, Yuekang Li, Ying Zhang, Leo Yu Zhang, Lida Zhao, Ji Jie, Yuxiao Lu
abstract: ArXiv:2605.28116v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mobile graphical user interface (GUI) agents driven by vision-language models (VLMs) perceive the screen as rendered pixels and choose actions from what they see, so they cannot reliably separate trusted interface elements from user-generated content. We present MIRAGE (Mobile Injection of Realistic Adversarial GUI Examples), a pipeline that turns benign mobile screenshots into prompt-injection samples by placing attacker-controlled text into ordinary user-generated content regions, without modifying the agent, the application, or the operating system. MIRAGE operates in three stages: a Localizer identifies user-controllable regions on the screenshot, a Generator synthesises context-aware payloads and renders them in the application's native style, and a Curator moderates realism and balances the samples across applications, region types, and attack intents. A key challenge is that an injected screenshot must stay visually indistinguishable from genuine user content while still diverting the agent; we address this by separating the stages that control reach, realism, and distributional balance. On a 1,111-sample benchmark spanning ten applications and eleven attack intents, all five evaluated VLM agents are vulnerable, with attack success rates of 23%-30%, and MIRAGE scores higher on human realism ratings than the strongest prior attack (3.02 versus 2.52 out of 5). We further find that per-sample realism and attack success are uncorrelated, so visual-quality filtering alone cannot reliably defend against this threat.
tldr: This paper presents a pipeline for generating context-aware prompt injection attacks against mobile GUI agents by embedding adversarial text into user-generated content regions.
motivation: Mobile GUI agents cannot distinguish trusted UI elements from user-generated content, making them vulnerable to prompt injection attacks that could lead to unintended actions.
method: The MIRAGE pipeline uses three stages: Localizer identifies user-controllable regions, Generator synthesizes context-aware payloads rendered in native style, and Curator ensures realism and balance across samples.
result: All five evaluated VLM agents achieved 23%-30% attack success rates on a 1,111-sample benchmark, and MIRAGE scored higher on human realism ratings than prior attacks (3.02 vs 2.52 out of 5).
conclusion: Prompt injection via user-generated content is a realistic threat to mobile GUI agents, and visual-quality filtering alone is insufficient as a defense.

title: Out Of Sight, Not Out Of Mind: Unveiling Latent Attack In Latent-based Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Chenxi Wang, Ruiyang Huang, Jiayan Sun, Lei Wei, Yifan Wu
abstract: ArXiv:2605.28214v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Latent-based multi-agent systems replace parts of explicit inter-agent communication with hidden representations, offering a new direction for efficient and flexible agent collaboration. However, moving coordination into latent space may also move attacks beyond the reach of visible-text inspection. In this paper, we study whether latent states can carry attack-associated information that remains effective during clean executions. To examine this question, we introduce a latent attack framework that reactivates attack-induced effects through latent interventions without reusing adversarial text. Extensive experiments show that the resulting latent-only attacks can substantially degrade task performance in clean executions, especially when applied to inter-agent KV-cache handoffs rather than local hidden states. Further control analyses indicate that this degradation cannot be reduced to arbitrary perturbations or invalid generation. Overall, our findings suggest that latent-based collaboration does not remove attack risk. It shifts part of the risk into less observable execution states, calling for safeguards beyond visible-text inspection.
tldr: This paper studies latent-space attacks in multi-agent systems, showing that adversarial effects can be embedded in hidden states and reactivated without visible text.
motivation: To investigate whether latent-based multi-agent collaboration introduces new security vulnerabilities that bypass visible-text inspection.
method: The authors propose a latent attack framework that reactivates attack-induced effects through latent interventions, applied to inter-agent KV-cache handoffs and local hidden states.
result: Latent-only attacks significantly degrade task performance, especially when targeting KV-cache handoffs, and the degradation is not due to arbitrary perturbations.
conclusion: Latent-based collaboration shifts attack risk into less observable states, necessitating new safeguards beyond visible-text inspection.

title: Generalizing Cdcl With Graph Backtracking
authors: Robin Coutelier, Thomas Hader, Laura Kov\'acs
abstract: ArXiv:2605.28220v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present graph backtracking, a novel, fine-grained backtracking scheme for CDCL-based SAT solving, parametrized by a user-defined weight function. For conflict repair, we challenge the decision level abstraction and use the implication graph as a precise guiding structure to minimize the weight of literals that are unassigned. Graph backtracking is sound and complete. We show that it is a generalization of chronological and non-chronological backtracking by simulating them with specific weight functions. Our approach is implemented in the experimental solver NapSAT. Empirical results show that graph backtracking requires fewer literal propagations than standard approaches, leading to improved solver runtime.
tldr: This paper introduces graph backtracking, a fine-grained backtracking scheme for CDCL-based SAT solving that uses the implication graph to minimize literal weight during conflict repair.
motivation: Standard CDCL solvers rely on decision level abstraction for backtracking, which may not be optimal. The authors aim to improve solver efficiency by using a more precise guiding structure.
method: The authors propose graph backtracking, parametrized by a user-defined weight function, which uses the implication graph to unassign literals with minimal weight. They implement it in the solver NapSAT and compare with standard approaches.
result: Graph backtracking requires fewer literal propagations than standard chronological and non-chronological backtracking, leading to improved solver runtime.
conclusion: Graph backtracking generalizes existing backtracking schemes and offers a new way to optimize SAT solving, with potential for further weight function designs.

title: Towards Cybersecurity SuperIntelligence (csi): What's The Best Harness For Cybersecurity?
authors: V\'ictor Mayoral-Vilches, Francesco Balassone, Mar\'ia Sanz-G\'omez, Paul Zabalegui Landa, Daniel S\'anchez Prieto, Marina Oteiza \'alvarez, Davide Quarta, Martin Pinzger
abstract: ArXiv:2605.28334v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: What is the best harness for cybersecurity AI? Cybersecurity systems are converging on a single execution scaffold per agent, an iterative shell loop driven by a Large Language Model (LLM). However, scaffolds are not interchangeable, rarely interoperable, and no single scaffold dominates across all challenge types. In our path towards researching Cybersecurity SuperIntelligence (CSI), we present a meta-scaffold that unifies heterogeneous agent harnesses under a common orchestration layer, enabling any LLM-driven scaffold to be deployed, benchmarked, and composed within the same infrastructure. Using CSI, we benchmark five scaffolds (CSI::Claude, CSI::Codex, CSI::GCAI, CSI::Mistral, CSI::CAI) on the 33 cybench challenges, holding the model fixed at alias2-mini. The best individual scaffolds solve 15/33 (45.5%); the four-scaffold union solves 17/33 (51.5%), with the fifth (CSI::Mistral, 10/33) contributing one exclusive solve. We find that no single scaffold is the best harness: it is the combination of structurally heterogeneous scaffolds that yields the highest coverage. We validate this through CSI's blackboard-based multi-agent architecture, in which scaffold-specialised agents run in parallel and exchange intermediate findings via a shared substrate (a blackboard). The blackboard solves 19/33 (57.6%), a 27% relative gain over CSI::Claude, one of the best individual scaffolds (15/33, 45.5%), 25% faster (20.2 h vs. 26.8 h), at comparable cost ([MATH]5,122).
tldr: This paper presents a meta-scaffold for unifying heterogeneous LLM-driven agent harnesses for cybersecurity challenges, but is unrelated to the user's research interests in quantum information, thermodynamics, or foundations.
motivation: The research aims to find the best harness for cybersecurity AI by comparing different LLM-driven scaffolds and proposing a multi-agent blackboard architecture.
method: The authors develop a meta-scaffold called CSI that orchestrates multiple agent harnesses (e.g., Claude, Codex) and benchmark them on 33 cybench challenges using a fixed LLM model.
result: The best individual scaffold solves 15/33 challenges; a union of four scaffolds solves 17/33; the blackboard multi-agent architecture solves 19/33, achieving a 27% relative gain over the best individual scaffold.
conclusion: No single scaffold dominates; combining heterogeneous scaffolds via a blackboard architecture improves coverage and efficiency, suggesting future work on multi-agent orchestration for cybersecurity.

title: Do You Dare To Try Test-Driven Forensics? Increasing Trust In Desktop Forensics With Adare
authors: Michael K\"ulper, Martin Lambertz, Mariia Rybalka
abstract: ArXiv:2605.28476v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Digital forensic relies on validated tools and established procedures, yet the underlying operating systems, applications, and analysis tools evolve rapidly. This evolution can cause artifact behavior and tool outputs to drift, silently degrading repeatability and confidence in long-lived forensic interpretations. We present test-driven forensics, a practical approach that treats forensic expectations as executable specifications: expected artifacts and expected tool outputs are encoded as tests that can be rerun across versions to detect regressions. Crucially, our approach also enables State Transition Testing, validating the system's expected state after each user action rather than only performing post-mortem checks on a final disk image; this supports causal attribution and makes transient behavior testable. We implement the methodology in ADARE, an open-source framework that runs controlled experiments in virtual machines and simulates realistic user activity via computer-vision-guided GUI automation. ADARE includes a companion web platform for sharing experiments, environments, and results to facilitate independent reruns and peer verification. We evaluate ADARE in five case studies spanning artifact research and tool validation. In particular, a 25-version regression study of Autopsy reveals substantial, largely undocumented changes in exported report outputs, demonstrating how executable tests make drift measurable and reproducible at scale.
tldr: This paper introduces test-driven forensics and the ADARE framework for desktop forensics, focusing on regression detection and state transition testing.
motivation: Digital forensic tools and operating systems evolve rapidly, causing silent drift in artifact behavior and tool outputs, which undermines repeatability and trust.
method: The authors propose encoding expected artifacts and tool outputs as executable tests, and implement State Transition Testing to validate system state after each user action. ADARE runs controlled experiments in VMs with GUI automation.
result: A 25-version regression study of Autopsy revealed substantial undocumented changes in exported report outputs, demonstrating that executable tests make drift measurable.
conclusion: Test-driven forensics improves trust and reproducibility in digital forensics; the ADARE framework and web platform facilitate sharing and independent verification.

title: Technical Report: Exploring The Emerging Threats Of The Agent Skill Ecosystem
authors: Luca Beurer-Kellner, Aleksei Kudrinskii, Marco Milanta, Kristian Bonde Nielsen, Hemang Sarkar, Liran Tal
abstract: ArXiv:2605.28588v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We analyzed 3,984 AI agent skills from major marketplaces and found 76 confirmed malicious payloads, including credential theft, backdoor installation, and data exfiltration. 13.4% of all skills contain at least one critical-level security issue and at least 8 manually confirmed malicious skills remain publicly available on clawhub.ai as of the date of publication. This report documents our methodology, presents a threat taxonomy based on real-world samples, and details the attack patterns we observed. As skill marketplaces grow rapidly and AI agents gain access to sensitive credentials and systems, automated security analysis is no longer optional.
tldr: This paper analyzes security threats in AI agent skill marketplaces, finding malicious payloads and critical security issues in a significant fraction of skills.
motivation: As AI agent skill marketplaces grow and agents gain access to sensitive systems, automated security analysis becomes necessary to identify and mitigate threats.
method: The authors analyzed 3,984 AI agent skills from major marketplaces, manually confirming malicious payloads and developing a threat taxonomy based on real-world samples.
result: They found 76 confirmed malicious payloads (credential theft, backdoor installation, data exfiltration), 13.4% of skills with critical-level security issues, and at least 8 malicious skills still publicly available.
conclusion: The findings highlight the urgent need for automated security analysis in AI agent skill ecosystems to prevent exploitation.

title: GraphSteal: Structural Knowledge Stealing From Graph Rag Via Traversal Reconstruction
authors: Jinze Gu, Qinghua Mao, Xi Lin, Jun Wu
abstract: ArXiv:2605.28645v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) enhances LLMs by grounding generation in query-relevant external evidence. Beyond unstructured text corpora, Graph RAG integrates knowledge graphs into the retrieval pipeline, enabling LLMs to access entities, relations, and multi-hop dependencies encoded in structured knowledge. However, the same structured knowledge that empowers Graph RAG also creates a new privacy attack surface. We demonstrate that Graph RAG systems can be turned into structural oracles: through adaptive black-box interactions, an adversary can elicit sufficient relational evidence to reconstruct substantial portions of the hidden knowledge graph. We propose a structure-oriented reconstruction framework that recovers targeted graphs from both local and global perspectives. Specifically, Depth-Wise Heuristic Search extracts fine-grained node attributes by recursively expanding entity-centered evidence, while Breadth-Wise Diffusion Search infers graph topology by propagating across relation-induced neighborhoods. Experiments on generic and healthcare scenarios demonstrate that our method can recover over 90\% of the original knowledge graph from representative Graph RAG systems, revealing sensitive entities, relations, and structural dependencies with high fidelity. Existing guradrails provide limited defense against our attack, highlighting the inherent difficulty of safeguarding structural privacy in Graph RAG pipelines.
tldr: This paper presents a method to steal knowledge graphs from Graph RAG systems via black-box traversal attacks.
motivation: Graph RAG systems use structured knowledge graphs to enhance LLM outputs, but this creates a privacy risk where adversaries can reconstruct the underlying graph.
method: The authors propose a two-phase attack: Depth-Wise Heuristic Search to extract node attributes and Breadth-Wise Diffusion Search to infer graph topology, both through adaptive black-box queries.
result: The attack recovers over 90% of the original knowledge graph from representative Graph RAG systems, revealing sensitive entities and relations with high fidelity.
conclusion: Existing guardrails are insufficient, highlighting the need for better structural privacy protections in Graph RAG pipelines.

title: Code As A Weapon: A Consensus-Labeled Prompt Bank For Measuring Coding-Model Compliance With Malicious-Code Requests
authors: Gregory D. Moody Richard J. Young
abstract: ArXiv:2605.28734v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A general-purpose language model that answers a harmful question returns text; a coding model that complies with a malicious request can return a working weapon -- a keylogger, a ransomware stub, an exploit that runs as written. This asymmetry in the severity of a single act of compliance implies coding-specialized models should clear a higher refusal bar than general-purpose chat models, not a lower one, yet the field cannot presently tell whether they do. Refusal benchmarks for malicious code are fragmented: they mix requests for executable software (ready-to-run weapons) with requests for harmful security knowledge (information a human must still operationalise) and report refusal rates over non-comparable corpora, so no single statistic measures the property that actually matters. This paper introduces an expanded consensus-labeled prompt bank that distinguishes between these two request types and provides a construct-stable substrate for cross-corpus coding-model compliance measurement. Eight corpora (ASTRA, CySecBench, AdvBench/harmful_behaviors, JailbreakBench, MalwareBench, RedCode, RMCBench, Scam2Prompt) are consolidated and classified under a five-judge consensus protocol (6,675 prompts x 5 judges = 33,375 calls). The panel reaches Fleiss' kappa = 0.767 [95% CI 0.755, 0.777] ("substantial"); 95.0% of prompts draw at least four agreeing judges, 76.9% are unanimous, and the panel reproduces the earlier four-corpus release at Cohen's kappa = 0.952 on the 3,133 shared prompts. The released bank comprises 4,748 consensus-CODE prompts (executable malicious code requests) and 1,923 consensus-KNOWLEDGE prompts (harmful security knowledge requests). The bank is the validated instrument the field has lacked: a reliability-quantified basis for testing whether coding models meet the stricter refusal standard their executable output demands.
tldr: This paper introduces a consensus-labeled prompt bank for measuring coding-model compliance with malicious-code requests, focusing on safety evaluation rather than quantum computing or information thermodynamics.
motivation: Current refusal benchmarks for malicious code are fragmented and mix executable software requests with harmful security knowledge, lacking a reliable metric for coding-model compliance.
method: The authors consolidated eight corpora (6,675 prompts) and used a five-judge consensus protocol to classify prompts into executable code requests (CODE) and knowledge requests (KNOWLEDGE), achieving substantial inter-rater reliability.
result: The panel reached Fleiss' kappa = 0.767, with 95% of prompts having at least four agreeing judges; the released bank contains 4,748 CODE and 1,923 KNOWLEDGE prompts.
conclusion: The prompt bank provides a validated instrument for testing whether coding models meet stricter refusal standards for executable outputs, but it is unrelated to the user's research interests in quantum information and thermodynamics.
